extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, public administrators, political scientists, and reformers
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and institutional design rules for creating independent intelligence/research bureaus within government, and for structuring expert input into public decision-making and public appeals. Covers funding, tenure, access, coordination, measurement, transparency, and procedure for deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of knowledge assembly from policy control
rubrics_metrics.description: The divorce between the assembling of knowledge and the control of policy should be as perfect as possible; experts must separate themselves from those who make decisions and not meddle with the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts must translate, simplify, generalize, but ensure that inferences apply to the real environment; if experts begin to take a line or 'have a policy' they are discounted. The power of the expert depends on not caring which decision is made; caring leads to seeing what one wishes to see and ceasing to see what one is there to see.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experts represent unseen elements and intangibles
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts should 'represent the unseen' — people who are not voters, events out of sight, relations between things and people; a constituency of intangibles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because intangibles cannot form a political majority, experts exercise influence by making the invisible visible and thereby altering the environment in which decision-makers act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional safeguard: separate executing staff from investigative staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate as absolutely as possible the staff which executes from the staff which investigates; they should be parallel but quite distinct bodies of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit differently, pay from separate funds if possible, make them responsible to different heads, and ensure intrinsic disinterest in each other's personal success to prevent absorption of decision functions by investigators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence depends on funds, tenure, and access
rubrics_metrics.description: Independence of intelligence officials turns mainly on three points: funds, tenure, and access to the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Congress or departmental officials can deprive them of money, dismiss them, or close the files, the staff becomes a creature of those authorities. Design must guard against those vulnerabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding independence and stability
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency of research cannot be really free if it depends on annual doles from a jealous or parsimonious congress; the financial arrangement should insure the staff against left-handed attacks and provide for growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed devices include a federal charter creating a trust fund, a sliding scale tied to departmental appropriations to cover overhead and minimum staff, and putting appropriation beyond accident so that attacks would have to be open and explicit rather than slyly destructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure tenure and professional dismissal safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenure should be for life with provision for retirement on a liberal pension, sabbatical years for advanced study and training, and dismissal only after a trial by professional colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply conditions common to non-profit intellectual careers to provide dignity, security, and freedom of mind; these qualities are necessary for salient, independent work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guaranteed access to materials and investigative powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Access to materials should be established in the organic act: the bureau should have the right to examine all papers and to question any official or outsider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuous investigation should be allowed without resembling sensational legislative inquiries; the bureau should be able to propose accounting methods to the department and, if rejected or violated, appeal under its charter to Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role as the connecting link between Congress and Departments
rubrics_metrics.description: Each intelligence bureau should serve as the connecting link between Congress and the Department — the Congressional eye on execution and the departmental answer to Congressional criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A permanent visible operation could reduce minute legislation born of distrust and thus make efficient administration easier by making departmental operation permanently visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparable standards and measurement across bureaus
rubrics_metrics.description: Various staffs should adopt standards of measurement that are comparable and exchange records so similar activities use the same measures and can be treated as competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparable accounting allows comparison and competition (e.g., when War Department and Post Office both buy lumber they can use the same measures), thereby making competition useful rather than chaotic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of index numbers and quantitative measures to guide competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Invent quantitative measures (index numbers) for qualities one wishes to promote (efficiency, productivity, service) so competition can be directed toward ideal ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better index numbers enable competition between workers, shops, factories, schools, government departments, military units, and political subdivisions; the consultation suggests employing index numbers broadly, not strictly in the technical sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central clearing house for interdepartmental information exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a central clearing house that assembles facts from different departments and supplies them in forms suited to diplomatic and administrative problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clearing house would become a focus of extraordinary information and tackle problems of definition, terminology, statistical technique, and logic, traversing the gamut of social sciences; most material (except a few secrets) could be open to scholars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration with universities and circulation of specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruit staff from college graduates, have part of the research done by students, associate political science in universities with practical politics, and enable a steady turnover of temporary and specialist appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A flexible association between a central agency and universities would create a national-university element, training and recruiting staff together, and providing exchange lecturers from Washington.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability to state, city, and county governments via federations
rubrics_metrics.description: The intelligence-principle applies to state governments, cities, and rural counties: work of comparison and interchange can occur by federations of state, city, and county bureaus with regional combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: So long as accounting systems are comparable, duplication can be avoided and regional coordination can reconcile autonomy of decision with cooperation for functions whose effective environments cross legal frontiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against dead weight and bureaucratic red tape
rubrics_metrics.description: A network of intelligence bureaus might become an irritation full of red tape, mountains of papers, forms, delays, lost documents, and pedants; there are no fool-proof institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risks are mitigated by circulation of personnel, data, and criticism among government, industry, offices, and universities; making the social process visible reduces trial-and-error and can reduce personnel per unit of result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose: aid to men of action and administrators, not burdening citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: The intelligence bureau is primarily an instrument for the man of action — the representative charged with decision and the worker at his work — to help them do public business better, not to burden every citizen with expert opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While serving as general information and a check on the press is secondary, its main value is to assist representative government and administration by supplying actionable analyses to insiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public judgment should focus on procedure rather than technical facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The general public can judge mostly whether procedures were sound before the event and whether relevant facts were duly considered; outsiders usually cannot decide what is relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public opinion's continuous action is essentially about procedure: whether interested groups were properly heard, ballots honestly taken, and results honestly accepted; citizens should insist problems pass through proper procedures before being presented to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use neutral chairmen/mediators to force evidence-based discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative discussions dealing with distant matters should be conducted in the presence of a neutral chairman or mediator who forces the discussion to address analyses supplied by experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partisan voices should appear but be confronted by men not personally involved who control facts and have dialectical skill; the chairman can call for wage tables, budgets, and official statistics to replace emotive declarations with concrete evidence, and can refer disputed technical points to federated intelligence bureaus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and enforceable demands for evidence in public conferences
rubrics_metrics.description: When a party asserts facts (e.g., that wages would 'ruin' a firm), the conference must require production of books and evidence; what is private does not interest the public tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If private data is withheld, the chairman issues public statements about the official facts and notes refusal to comply; disputed methodological claims can be referred to standing committees of federated intelligence bureaus for adjudication.
